title: Digits, Place Value & Number Bases
coreInsight: A numeral is a weighted sum of its digits; changing the base changes the place-value weights but not the underlying positional idea.
targetLearnerRealization: A numeral is a weighted sum of its digits, so digit constraints and alternate bases can be translated into algebraic place-value structure.
learningObjectives: Distinguish a digit symbol from the value of the numeral containing it.
Expand a positional numeral as a weighted sum and explain the role of zero.
Interpret and convert numerals in bases other than ten using powers of the base.
Optimize digit placement by assigning larger digits to larger positional weights.

continuity.openingCallback: Use magnitude to predict how moving one digit between place-value columns changes a number.
closingSeeds: Weighted-position reasoning turns digit arrangements and alternate-base numerals into ordinary algebraic sums.

misconceptionTargets.misconception: A digit and the number it appears in are the same kind of object.
A leading zero creates a genuinely new place-value length.
Digit optimization can ignore positional weights.
Base-b numerals should still be interpreted with powers of 10.

beats.purpose: Create the need for positional weights by swapping two fixed digit symbols.
beats.expectedRealization: Moving 5 from tens to ones and 2 from ones to tens decreases the number by 27 because the positions carry different weights.
beats.transitionIn: Magnitude predicts that moving a larger digit right should make a number smaller. Measure exactly how the place weights cause the change.
beats.transitionOut: The digit symbols stayed 5 and 2, but their contributions changed from 50+2 to 20+5.
beats.whyNow: A digit swap separates symbol identity from positional value before formal expansion.
beats.entryBridge: Compare only the tens and ones contributions in 352 and 325; the hundreds contribution is unchanged.
beats.reusedRepresentation: Digit tiles placed in weighted hundreds, tens, and ones columns.
learnerPrompts: Which place stayed unchanged?
What value did each moved digit contribute before and after?

visual.ariaLabel: Place-value contributions of the digits in three hundred fifty-two and three hundred twenty-five

steps.body: The shared 3 contributes 300 in both numerals.
The changed part drops from 5×10+2 = 52 to 2×10+5 = 25, a decrease of 27.

resolution.takeaway: A digit's contribution is its symbol value multiplied by its place weight.

beats.purpose: Distinguish digit symbols, numerals, and numerical values.
beats.expectedRealization: The digit 5 is a symbol; within 352 it contributes value 50; the numeral 352 names the entire number.
beats.transitionIn: Name the different objects that appeared in the swap.
beats.prompt: Which statement correctly distinguishes the digit 5 from the numeral 352?

options.text: 5 is one digit symbol; in 352 it contributes 50, while 352 is the whole numeral.
The digit 5 and the number 352 are the same kind of object.
The digit 5 always contributes value 5 wherever it appears.
352 is a single digit.

beats.correctFeedback: Right—a digit is a symbol whose numerical contribution depends on position.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Separate the written character, its weighted contribution, and the full numeral.

steps.body: In 352, the symbol 5 occupies the tens place, so its contribution is 5×10=50. The whole numeral has value 300+50+2.

resolution.takeaway: Digits are symbols; positional weights turn their arrangement into a number.

beats.purpose: Explain why a leading zero does not create a new place-value length.
beats.expectedRealization: A leading zero contributes zero times its weight, so 0352 and 352 have the same value and standard numeral length.
beats.transitionIn: Place a zero in a new column to the left and inspect its contribution.
beats.prompt: What does the leading zero do in 0352?

options.text: It contributes 0×1000, so the value remains 352 and the standard numeral is still three-digit.
It creates a different four-digit number.
It multiplies 352 by 10.
It makes the entire numeral equal to 0.

beats.correctFeedback: Exactly—the written padding changes, but the weighted sum does not.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Compute the contribution of the thousands digit: 0×1000.

steps.body: 0352 = 0×1000+3×100+5×10+2 = 352. Standard positional notation omits leading zero columns.

resolution.takeaway: A zero inside a numeral holds a place; a leading zero adds no new numerical length.

beats.purpose: Formalize familiar decimal notation as a weighted sum.
beats.expectedRealization: Each decimal place uses a power of 10, and the numeral is the sum of digit-times-weight contributions.
beats.transitionIn: The swap and leading-zero examples follow one rule across every decimal column.
beats.name: Positional notation
beats.conciseDefinition: A positional numeral represents the sum of each digit multiplied by the weight of its place.
beats.memoryHook: Digit times place weight, then add.

beats.purpose: Generalize decimal place weights through concrete bundles of five.
beats.expectedRealization: In base five, the place weights are 25,5,1, so (243)₅ equals 73 in decimal.
beats.transitionIn: Keep the positional rule but replace bundles of ten with bundles of five.
beats.prompt: A base-five numeral (243)₅ has 2 bundles of 25, 4 bundles of 5, and 3 ones. What decimal value does it represent?

resolution.takeaway: Changing the base changes the weights, not the digit-times-weight structure.

beats.purpose: State the general base-b weighted-sum rule.
beats.expectedRealization: A base-b numeral uses powers of b and digits from 0 through b−1.
beats.transitionIn: The decimal and base-five expansions are instances of one positional pattern.
beats.name: Base-b numeral
beats.conciseDefinition: In base b, place weights are …,b³,b²,b,1, and every digit is an integer from 0 through b−1.
beats.memoryHook: Replace powers of ten with powers of the base.

beats.purpose: Connect the base to its allowed digit symbols.
beats.expectedRealization: Base six has digits 0 through 5, so a written digit 7 is invalid.
beats.transitionIn: A bundle is carried whenever a count reaches the base, so no single digit can equal or exceed the base.
beats.prompt: Which proposed base-six numeral is invalid?
beats.incorrectFeedback: Compare every written digit with the base 6.

steps.body: A digit 7 would be regrouped into one six plus one, so it cannot occupy a single base-six place.

resolution.takeaway: Valid base-b digits lie from 0 through b−1.

beats.purpose: Contrast an additive symbol system with positional read-off and expose the required zero placeholder.
beats.expectedRealization: The symbols total 10,423; the missing thousands symbol becomes a zero when the additive total is written positionally.
beats.transitionIn: A different numeral system assigns fixed values to symbols and adds them; translate its total back into positional decimal notation.
beats.transitionOut: The absent thousands contribution did not erase the ten-thousands place; it became the internal zero in 10,423.
beats.whyNow: The approved additional problem provides a low-load contrast between additive symbols and positional columns while reinforcing the role of an empty place.
beats.entryBridge: Group identical symbols, multiply each count by its fixed value, and add the contributions.
beats.exitBridge: When writing the sum in decimal columns, retain a zero for the missing thousands contribution.
beats.reusedRepresentation: Value groups collapsing into a place-value strip.
learnerPrompts: What fixed value does each symbol contribute?
Which place has no symbol contribution?
How must that empty place appear in decimal notation?
beats.incorrectFeedback: Add 10,000+400+20+3 and keep an internal zero for the thousands place.

steps.body: There is no thousands contribution, so positional decimal notation uses a zero in that internal place.

resolution.takeaway: An empty internal place needs a zero placeholder when an additive total is written positionally.

beats.purpose: Clarify that order behaves differently in additive and positional numeral systems.
beats.expectedRealization: Fixed-value additive symbols may be reordered without changing the sum, while digit order changes positional weights.
beats.transitionIn: Compare the symbol grouping with the earlier 352-to-325 swap.
beats.prompt: Why did reordering 5 and 2 change 352, while reordering Egyptian symbols would not change their total?

options.text: Decimal digits inherit value from position; each Egyptian symbol keeps a fixed value wherever it is written.
Both systems are positional in exactly the same way.
Only systems containing zero depend on order.
Reordering matters only for numbers above 100.

beats.correctFeedback: Exactly—positional order assigns weights, while additive symbols carry fixed weights themselves.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Ask whether moving a symbol changes the weight multiplying it.

steps.body: In 352, moving 5 changes its multiplier from 10 to 1. An additive 100-symbol remains worth 100 wherever it appears.

resolution.takeaway: Always identify whether position or symbol type supplies the weight.

beats.purpose: Derive the optimization rule from a two-position exchange.
beats.expectedRealization: Assigning the larger digit to the larger weight maximizes the total contribution.
beats.transitionIn: Use the swap calculation as a proof tool for arranging digits.
beats.name: Exchange principle
beats.conciseDefinition: If x>y and W>w, then xW+yw is greater than xw+yW by (x−y)(W−w).

beats.purpose: Optimize ten digit placements across two five-digit numbers by place weight.
beats.expectedRealization: The two largest digits occupy the two ten-thousands positions, the next pair the thousands positions, and so on; only 87431 fits one digit from every required pair.
beats.transitionIn: Two numbers share each positional weight, so assign digits in descending pairs from the largest weight to the smallest.
beats.transitionOut: The valid number 87431 pairs with 96520, and their place-by-place digit sums maximize the total.
beats.whyNow: The approved transfer makes positional weights decisive across a global digit arrangement and rewards a proof by exchanges rather than visual guesswork.
beats.entryBridge: Pair {9,8} with ten-thousands, {7,6} with thousands, {5,4} with hundreds, {3,2} with tens, and {1,0} with ones.
beats.exitBridge: Check each proposed number for exactly one digit from each pair in the matching position.
beats.reusedRepresentation: Place-value columns with digit pairs assigned by descending weight.
learnerPrompts: Which two positions carry the largest equal weight?
Which digit pair must occupy them?
Which choice takes one digit from every required pair in order?
beats.correctFeedback: Correct—87431 can pair with 96520 to achieve the maximum sum.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Check each place against the required pairs {9,8}, {7,6}, {5,4}, {3,2}, {1,0}.

steps.body: An exchange argument places the two largest digits in the two ten-thousands slots, then the next two in the thousands slots, continuing downward.
Only 87431 takes one digit from each required pair in the correct column.
Its complement 96520 uses the other digits, and 87431+96520=183951.

resolution.takeaway: Optimize positional numerals by matching the largest available digits to the largest weights.

beats.purpose: Assess digit contribution in decimal notation.
beats.expectedRealization: In 5082, the digit 8 occupies the tens place and contributes 80.
beats.transitionIn: Separate one digit symbol from its weighted contribution.
beats.transitionOut: The symbol 8 is multiplied by place weight 10.
beats.whyNow: A near item checks the foundational distinction independently.
beats.exitBridge: Multiply the digit by that column's weight.
learnerPrompts: Which place contains 8?
What is its contribution to the whole number?
beats.incorrectFeedback: The 8 is one column left of the ones place, so its weight is 10.

resolution.takeaway: A digit's value in a numeral is digit times place weight.

beats.purpose: Assess leading-zero meaning and numeral length.
beats.expectedRealization: 0074 has value 74 and is not a four-digit standard numeral.
beats.transitionIn: Inspect padded notation without inventing new magnitude.
beats.transitionOut: Both leading columns contribute zero, so the first nonzero digit determines the standard length.
beats.whyNow: A near item directly repairs the leading-zero misconception.
beats.entryBridge: Expand every written place, including the zeros.
beats.exitBridge: Remove zero-contribution columns on the left.
learnerPrompts: What do the two leading digits contribute?
Where is the first nonzero digit?
beats.correctFeedback: Correct—0074 has value 74 and standard length two.

steps.body: 0074=0+0+70+4=74. The leading zeros are padding, not new magnitude.

resolution.takeaway: Leading zeros do not change value or standard digit length.

beats.purpose: Assess expansion of a base-five numeral.
beats.transitionIn: Use powers of five rather than familiar decimal weights.
beats.whyNow: A mixed item checks correct base-dependent weights.
beats.exitBridge: Add the weighted contributions in decimal.
learnerPrompts: What are the three place weights?
What does each digit contribute?

resolution.takeaway: Evaluate a base-b numeral with powers of b, not powers of ten.

beats.purpose: Assess conversion from decimal into base five by successive place filling.
beats.expectedRealization: Ninety-four uses 3 twenty-fives, 3 fives, and 4 ones, so it is (334)₅.
beats.transitionIn: Reverse the weighted sum by filling the largest base-five places first.
beats.transitionOut: The coefficients 3,3,4 are all valid base-five digits and reconstruct 94.
beats.whyNow: A mixed item reverses the conversion direction.
beats.entryBridge: Take as many 25s as possible, then 5s, then ones.
beats.exitBridge: Reconstruct the decimal value to check.
learnerPrompts: How many groups of 25 fit?
How many groups of 5 fit in the remainder?
What ones remain?

steps.body: Three 25s use 75 and leave 19. Three 5s use 15 and leave 4.

resolution.takeaway: Conversion fills base-power places from largest to smallest and checks by reconstruction.

beats.purpose: Assess digit optimization under nondecimal positional weights.
beats.expectedRealization: The descending arrangement (641)₇ is largest and has decimal value 323.
beats.transitionIn: For the final challenge, apply the exchange principle where the weights are 49,7,1.
beats.transitionOut: Matching 6,4,1 to descending weights maximizes the numeral; its value is 323.
beats.whyNow: The challenge unifies base conversion and positional optimization.
beats.entryBridge: Order digits by size and place weights by size, then pair them.
beats.exitBridge: Evaluate the resulting base-seven weighted sum.
learnerPrompts: Which digit belongs with weight 49?
Which arrangement is largest?
What decimal value does it represent?
beats.incorrectFeedback: Place 6 with 7², 4 with 7, and 1 with 1; then evaluate.

steps.body: The exchange principle puts 6,4,1 against weights 49,7,1, so (641)₇ is largest.

resolution.takeaway: The large-digit/large-weight rule works in every positional base.

beats.purpose: Consolidate object distinctions, zero, base weights, and optimization.
beats.expectedRealization: One weighted-sum model explains decimal notation, alternate bases, and digit placement.
beats.transitionIn: Digit swaps, empty places, symbol systems, and new bases can now be checked by the same questions.
beats.prompt: Which statements belong in reliable place-value reasoning? Select all four.

options.text: Distinguish a digit symbol from its weighted contribution and the whole numeral.
Use zero to hold an empty internal place; ignore leading zero contributions.
Use powers of the stated base and digits below that base.
For maximization, pair larger digits with larger positional weights.
Interpret every numeral using powers of 10 regardless of its base.

response.feedback: Track the symbol, its weight, zero places, the stated base, and any optimization objective.

beats.correctFeedback: Exactly—those four checks preserve the positional structure.
beats.incorrectFeedback: The place weights are powers of the stated base, which need not be ten.

resolution.takeaway: A numeral is a weighted sum; identify the weights before calculating or arranging digits.

beats.purpose: Connect place-value structure to algebraic modeling.
beats.expectedRealization: Digit and base constraints can be translated into coefficients and powers in a weighted sum.
beats.transitionIn: Writing a numeral as a sum makes its hidden positional structure explicit.
beats.prompt: When a problem constrains digits, swaps positions, or changes the base, which weighted-sum expression would expose exactly what changes and what stays fixed?
beats.takeaway: Translate the numeral into digit-times-weight terms; then use ordinary arithmetic or algebra on the visible structure.

notes: Draft foundation lesson authored from the approved N7 compact context packet.
A decimal digit swap establishes weighted contributions before the rule generalizes to base five and base b.
The approved 2025 additive-numeral problem supplies a contrast and empty-place application; the approved 2012 problem is the mapped optimization transfer.
All generated answers were independently checked by weighted-sum expansion and a separate subtraction, regrouping, reconstruction, or exchange argument.
No lesson-specific renderer infrastructure was added.
